doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Back in Indianapolis after Snookum Russell: Beryl Steiner and living at home
summary: With the band broken up he sat in around town, discussed alto player Beryl Steiner, and lived with his parents.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: It's my understanding then that Snookum Russell’s band broke up. Did you go directly to Benny Carter after Snookum Russell’s band broke up?

No, I came back to Indianapolis and just kind of wandered around as an unemployed musician. I recall that I was able to sit in with – I don’t know who was prominent or active, I should say, at that time as far as Indianapolis bands were concerned – but I remember playing with either [Jimmy] Coe or maybe LaVon Kemp was still around. I don’t just remember. I’m a little fuzzy there.
Was Syd Valentine here? And the alto player who later on owned a hair place? I just wondered if those were . . .
That name does not ring a bell. No, it doesn’t.
Beryl Steiner.
Oh, that name rings a bell.
I wondered if you . . .
A good – an excellent player.
Yes. A first-rate player.
A beautiful player.
I wondered if that was somebody you encountered, because he was playing here.
Beryl Steiner. His approach and his style reminded one a lot of the – what was the lead alto player with Lunceford?
Willie?
Willie.
Willie.
Willie Smith. He played with that kind of approach.
Yeah, I remember that.
Did he not? Yes, he did. He did. I think he patterned himself, he wanted to pattern himself after him.
When you were between working with Snookum Russell and before you went with Benny Carter, what kinds of things did you do to support yourself and yet be able to stay musically active?
I lived with my mother and father. I didn’t support myself. I lived in their house and ate their food. [laughs] That’s how. That’s how that came about. I lived with mom and dad.
